{{Short description|Special labeling in graph theory}}
In [[graph theory]], the act of [[Graph coloring|coloring]] generally implies the assignment of labels to [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]], [[Glossary of graph theory terms#edge|edges]] or [[Glossary of graph theory terms#face|faces]] in a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]. The '''incidence coloring''' is a special [[graph labeling]] where each [[Incidence (graph)|incidence]] of an edge with a vertex is assigned a color under certain constraints.

==Definitions==
Below ''G'' denotes a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|simple graph]] with non-empty vertex [[Set (mathematics)|set]] (non-empty) ''V''(''G''), edge set ''E''(''G'') and [[Degree (graph theory)|maximum degree]] Δ(''G'').

'''Definition.''' An [[incidence (graph)|'''incidence''']] is defined as a pair (''v'', ''e'') where <math>v\in V(G)</math> is an end point of <math>e\in E(G).</math> In simple words, one says that vertex ''v'' is incident to edge ''e''. Two incidences (''v'', ''e'') and (''u'', ''f'') are said to be '''adjacent''' or '''neighboring''' if one of the following holds:
* ''v'' = ''u'', ''e'' ≠ ''f''
* ''e'' = ''f'', ''v'' ≠ ''u''
* ''e'' = {''v'', ''u''}, ''f'' = {''u'', ''w''} and ''v'' ≠ ''w''.

[[File:Neighborly Incidences.jpg|thumb|centre|upright=3|Examples of adjacent/neighboring incidences. The * above the edge e closest to vertex v denotes incidence (v,e).]]

'''Definition.''' Let ''I''(''G'') be the set of all incidences of ''G''. An incidence coloring of ''G'' is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>c: I(G)\to\N</math> that takes distinct values on adjacent incidences (we use the simplified notation ''c''(''v'', ''u'') is used instead of ''c''((''v'', ''e'')).) The minimum number of colors needed for the incidence coloring of a graph ''G'' is known as the '''incidence chromatic number''' or '''incidence coloring number''' of ''G'', represented by <math>\chi_i(G).</math> This notation was introduced by [[Jennifer Quinn|Jennifer J. Quinn Massey]] and [[Richard A. Brualdi]] in 1993.

[[File:Incidence coloring example.jpg|thumb|centre|upright=1.5|Incidence coloring of a [[Petersen graph]]]]

==History==
The concept of incidence coloring was introduced by Brualdi and Massey in 1993 who bounded it in terms of Δ(''G''). Initially, the incidence chromatic number of trees, complete bipartite graphs and complete graphs was found out. They also conjectured that all graphs can have an incidence coloring using Δ(''G'') + 2 colors (Incidence coloring conjecture - ICC). This conjecture was disproved by Guiduli, who showed that incidence coloring concept is a directed star arboricity case,<ref>Algor I., Alon N. (1989); "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0012365X89900733 The star arboricity of graphs]", Discrete Mathematics 75, pp. 11-22.</ref> introduced by [[Noga Alon|Alon]] and Algor. His counter example showed that incidence chromatic number is at most Δ(''G'') + O(log Δ(''G'')).<ref name='gb'>Guiduli B. (1997); "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0012365X9500342T On incidence coloring and star arboricity of graphs]", Discrete Mathematics 163, pp. 275-278</ref>

Chen et al. found the incidence chromatic number of [[Path (graph theory)|paths]], fans, [[Cycle graph|cycles]], wheels, complete tripartite graph and adding edge wheels. Few years later, Shiu et al. showed that this conjecture is true for certain [[cubic graph]]s such as cubic Hamiltonian graphs. He showed that in case of outerplanar graph of maximum degree 4, the incidence chromatic number is not 5. The bounds for incidence chromatic number of various graph classes is found out now.

==Basic results==
:'''Proposition.''' <math>\chi_i(G) \ge \Delta(G)+1.</math>

'''Proof.''' Let ''v'' be the vertex with maximum degree Δ in ''G''. Let <math>e_1, e_2,\ldots, e_\Delta</math> be the edges that are incident with the vertex ''v''. Consider <math>e_1 =\{v, w\}.</math> We can see that every pair of Δ + 1 incidences, that is, <math>(v,e_1), (v,e_2), \ldots, (v, e_\Delta), (w, e_1)</math> is neighborly. Therefore, these incidences have to be colored using distinct colors.

The bound is attained by trees and complete graphs:

* If ''G'' is a [[complete graph]] with at least two vertices then <math>\chi_i(G)=\Delta(G)+1.</math>
* If ''G'' is a tree with at least two vertices then <math>\chi_i(G)=\Delta(G)+1.</math>

The main results were proved by Brualdi and Massey (1993). Shiu, Sun and Wu have proposed certain necessary conditions for graph satisfying <math>\chi_i(G)=\Delta(G)+1.</math>

* <math>\chi_i(G) \le 2\Delta(G).</math>
* The incidence chromatic number of the [[complete bipartite graph]] <math>K_{m,n}</math> with ''m'' ≥ ''n'' ≥ 2, is ''m'' + 2.
* <math>\chi_i(C_n) \le 4</math> and <math>\chi_i(C_{3n})= 3.</math>

==Incidence coloring of some graph classes==
===Meshes===
Several algorithms are introduced to provide incidence coloring of meshes<ref>Huang, C. I.; Wang, Y. L.; Chung, S. S. (2004), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0898122104004171 The Incidence Coloring Numbers of Meshes]", Computers and Mathematics with Applications 48, pp. 1643–1649</ref> like [[Lattice graph|square meshes]], honeycomb meshes and hexagonal meshes. These algorithms are optimal. For each mesh, the incidence colors can be made in the linear time with the fewest colors. It is found out that ∆(''G'') + 1 colors are required for incidence coloring of square meshes, honeycomb meshes and hexagonal meshes.

* The incidence chromatic number of a square mesh is 5.
* The incidence chromatic number of a hexagonal mesh is 7.
* The incidence chromatic number of a honeycomb mesh is 4.

===Halin graphs===
Chen, Wang and Pang proved that if ''G'' is a [[Halin graph]] with ∆(''G'') > 4 then <math>\chi_i(G) =\Delta(G)+1.</math> For Halin graphs with ∆(''G'') = 3 or 4, Jing-Zhe Qu showed <math>\chi_i(G)</math> to be 5 or 6 respectively. Whether the incidence coloring number of Halin graphs with low degree is Δ(''G'') + 1 is still an unsolved problem.

Shiu and Sun proved every cubic Halin graph other than <math>K_4</math> has an incidence coloring with Δ(''G'') + 2 colors. Su, Meng and Guo extended this result to all pseudo-Halin graphs.

If the Halin graph ''G'' contains a [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] ''T'', then <math>\chi_i(G^2) \le \Delta(T^2) +\Delta(T) +8.</math><ref>Wang, S. D.; Cheng, D. L.; Pang, S. C. (2002), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X01003028 The incidence coloring number of Halin graphs and outerplanar graphs]", Discrete Mathematics 256, pp. 397–405</ref>

===k-degenerated graphs===
D.L. Chen, P.C.B. Lam and W.C. Shiu had conjectured that the incidence chromatic number of a cubic graph ''G'' is at most ∆(''G'') + 2. They proved this for certain cubic graphs such as Hamiltonian cubic graphs. Based on these results, M. H. Dolama, E. Sopena and X. Zhu (2004) studied the graph classes for which <math>\chi_i(G)</math> is bounded by ∆(''G'') + ''c'' where ''c'' is some fixed constant.<ref name=dsz>Hosseini Dolama, M.; Sopena, E.; Zhu, X. (2004), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X04001517 Incidence coloring of k-generated graphs]", Discrete Mathematics 283, pp. 121–128</ref> A graph is said to be ''k''-generated if for every subgraph ''H'' of ''G'', the minimum degree of ''H'' is at most ''k''.

* Incidence chromatic number of ''k''-degenerated graphs ''G'' is at most ∆(''G'') + 2''k'' − 1.
* Incidence chromatic number of ''K''<sub>4</sub> minor free graphs ''G'' is at most ∆(''G'') + 2 and it forms a tight bound.
* Incidence chromatic number of a planar graph ''G'' is at most ∆(''G'') + 7.

===Outerplanar graphs===
Consider an [[outerplanar graph]] ''G'' with [[Biconnected component|cut vertex]] ''v'' such that ''G'' – ''v'' is the [[Graph operations|union]] of <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math>. Let <math>G_1</math> (resp. <math>G_2</math>) be the [[Glossary of graph theory|induced subgraph]] on vertex ''v'' and vertices of <math>H_1</math> (resp. <math>H_2</math>). Then <math>\chi_i(G)</math> is the maximum of <math>\chi_i(G_1), \chi_i(G_2)</math> and <math>1+d_G(v)</math> where <math>d_G(v)</math> is the degree of vertex ''v'' in ''G''.

The incidence chromatic number of an outerplanar graph ''G'' is at most ∆(''G'') + 2. In case of outerplanar graphs with ∆(''G'') > 3 the incidence chromatic number is ∆(''G'') + 1.

Since outerplanar graphs are ''K''<sub>4</sub>-minor-free graphs, they accept a (Δ + 2, 2)–incidence coloring.<ref name=dsz /><ref>Wang, S.; Xu, J.; Ma, F.; Xu, C. (2008), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1002007108000610 The (Δ + 2, 2)-incidence coloring of outerplanar graphs]", Progress in Natural Science 18, pp. 575–578.</ref> The solution for incidence chromatic number of the outerplanar graph ''G'' having Δ(''G'') = 3 and [[Connectivity (graph theory)|2-connected]] outerplanar graph is still an open question.

===Chordal rings===
Chordal rings are variations of ring networks. The use of chordal rings in communication is very extensive due to its advantages over the interconnection networks with ring topology and other analysed structures such as meshes, hypercubes, Cayley's graphs, etc. Arden and Lee<ref>Arden B.W., Lee H. (1981); "[https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpls/abs_all.jsp?arnumber=1675777 Analysis of Chordal Ring Network]", IEEE Transactions on Computers 30, pp. 291-295.</ref> first proposed the chordal ring of degree 3, that is, the ring structured network in which every node has an extra link known as chord, to some other node in the network. Distributed loop networks are chordal rings of degree 4 which is constructed by adding 2 extra chords at every vertex in a [[ring network]].

The chordal ring on ''N'' nodes and chord length ''d'', denoted by ''CR''(''N'',''d''), is a graph defined as:

:<math>\begin{align} 
V(G)&=\{v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{N-1}\} \\
E(G)&= \{ v_iv_j : i-j \equiv 1,d \bmod N\}
\end{align}</math>

These graphs are studied due to their application in communication. Kung-Fu Ding, Kung-Jui Pai and Ro-Yu Wu studied the incidence coloring of chordal rings.<ref>Ding K.F., Pai K.J., Yu R. (1981); "[http://par.cse.nsysu.edu.tw/~algo/paper/paper15/A2_4.pdf Some Results on the Incidence Coloring Number of Chordal Rings*]", The 32nd Workshop on Combinatorial Mathematics and Computation Theory, pp. 89-93.</ref> Several algorithms are formulated to find the incidence chromatic number of chordal rings. The major findings are:

:<math>\begin{align}
\chi_i(CR(N,2)) &= \begin{cases} 5 & 5|N \\ 6 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
\chi_i(CR(N,3)) &= \begin{cases} 5 & 5|N \\ 6 & N \equiv 2 \bmod 5\end{cases}
\end{align}</math>

===Powers of cycles===
Keaitsuda Nakprasit and Kittikorn Nakprasit studied the incidence coloring of powers of cycles, <math>C_n^k.</math> If 2''k'' + 1 ≥ ''n'' then <math>C_n^k = K_n</math> so assume ''n'' > 2''k'' + 1 and write:

:<math> n = (2k+1)t + r, \quad 1 \leq t, \quad 0 \leq r \leq 2k.</math>

Their results can be summarized as follows:<ref name='nk'>Nakprasit, Keaitsuda and Nakprasit, Kittikorn (2012), "[http://www.ijpam.eu/contents/2012-76-1/13/13.pdf Incidence colorings of the powers of cycles]", International Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics 76(1), pp. 143–148</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
\chi_i(C_n^k) &= \begin{cases} 2k+1 & r =0 \\ 2k+2 & 1 \leq r \leq t \text{ or } r =2k\end{cases} && k \geq 3 \\
\chi_i(C_n^2) &= \begin{cases} 5 & 5|n \\ 6 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{align}</math>

The relation to incidence coloring conjecture is given by the observation that <math>\Delta(C_n^k) = 2k.</math>

==Relation between incidence chromatic number and domination number of a graph==
:'''Proposition.'''<ref name='sk'>Sun, P. K. (2012), "[http://journal.taiwanmathsoc.org.tw/index.php/TJM/article/view/2642/1427 Incidence coloring of regular graphs and complement graphs]", Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics 16, No. 6, pp. 2289–2295</ref> Let ''G'' be a simple connected graph of order ''n'', size ''m'' and domination number <math>\gamma.</math> Then <math>\chi_i(G) \ge \tfrac{2m}{n-\gamma}.</math>

'''Proof.''' Form a [[Directed graph|digraph]] ''D''(''G'') from graph ''G'' by dividing each edge of ''G'' into 2 arcs in opposite directions. We can see that the total number of arcs in ''D''(''G'') is 2''m''. According to Guiduli,<ref name='gb' /> the incidence coloring of ''G'' is equivalent to proper coloring of the digraph ''D''(''G''), where 2 distinct arcs <math>\overrightarrow{u v}</math> and <math>\overrightarrow{x y}</math> are adjacent if one of the following conditions holds: (i) ''u'' = ''x''; (ii) ''v'' = ''x'' or ''y'' = ''u''. By the definition of adjacency of arcs, an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of arcs in ''D''(''G'') is a star forest. Therefore, a maximal independent set of arcs is a maximal star [[Tree (graph theory)|forest]]. This implies that at least <math>\tfrac{2m}{n-\gamma}</math> color classes are required.<ref name='sk' />

This relation has been widely used in the characterization of (''r'' + 1)-incidence colorable ''r''-regular graphs. The major result on incidence coloring of ''r''-regular graphs is: If graph ''G'' is [[Regular graph|r-regular graph]], then <math>\chi_{i}(G) = \chi_{i}(G^2)=r+1</math> if and only if ''V''(''G'') is a disjoint union of ''r'' + 1 [[dominating set]]s.<ref name='sk' />

==Interval incidence coloring==
'''Definition.''' A finite subset <math>A\subset\N</math> is an '''interval''' [[if and only if]] it contains all the numbers between its minimum and its maximum.

'''Definition.''' Let ''c'' to be an incidence coloring of ''G'' and define

:<math>A_c (v) = \{c(v,e) : (v,e) \in I(G) \}.</math>

An '''interval incidence coloring''' of ''G'' is an incidence coloring ''c'' such that for each vertex ''v'' of ''G'' the set <math>A_c(v)</math> is an interval.<ref>Janczewski, R.; Malafiejska, A.; Malafiejski, M., "Interval Wavelength Assignment in All-optical Star Networks", Parallel Processing and Applied Mathematics, 8th International Conference, PPAM 2009, Wtroclaw, Poland, September 13–16, 2009. Revised Selected Papers Part I (Springer), pp. 11–20, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-14390-8_2, {{ISBN|978-3-642-14389-2}}</ref><ref>Janczewski, R.; Małafiejska, A.; Małafiejski, M. (2015), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X14001292 Interval incidence graph coloring]", Discrete Applied Mathematics 182, pp. 73–83</ref> The '''interval incidence coloring number''' of ''G'' is the minimum number of colors used for the interval incidence coloring of ''G''. It is denoted by <math>\chi_{ii}.</math> It is clear that <math>\chi_{i}(G) \le \chi_{ii}(G).</math> If only <math>\chi_{ii}</math> colors are used for the interval incidence coloring, then it is said to be minimal.

The concept of interval incidence coloring was introduced by A. Malafiejska, R. Janczewski and M. Malafiejski. They proved <math>\chi_{ii}(G) \le \Delta(G)</math> for bipartite graphs.<ref>Janczewski, R.; Małafiejska, A.; Małafiejski, M. (2014), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X13004356 Interval incidence coloring of bipartite graphs]", Discrete Applied Mathematics 166, pp. 131–145</ref> In case of regular bipartite graphs equality holds. Subcubic bipartite graphs admit an interval incidence coloring using four, five or six colors. They have also proved incidence 5-colorability can be decided in linear time for bipartite graphs with ∆(''G'') = 4.

==Fractional incidence coloring==
The fractional version of the incidence coloring was first introduced by Yang in 2007. An ''r''-[[tuple]] incidence ''k''-coloring of a graph ''G'' is the assignment of ''r'' colors to each incidence of graph ''G'' from a set of ''k'' colors such that the adjacent incidences are given [[disjoint sets]] of colors.<ref>Yang, D (2012), "[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/267173229_Fractional_incidence_coloring_and_star_arboricity_of_graphs Fractional incidence coloring and star arboricity of graphs]", Ars Combinatoria - Waterloo then Winnipeg 105, pp. 213–224</ref> By definition, it is obvious that 1-tuple incidence ''k''-coloring is an incidence ''k''-coloring too.

The fractional incidence chromatic number of graph ''G'' is the infimum of the fractions <math>\tfrac{k}{r}</math> in such a way that ''G'' admits a ''r''-tuple incidence ''k''-coloring. Fractional incidence coloring has great applications in several fields of computer science. Based on incidence coloring results by Guiduli,<ref name='gb' /> Yang has proved that the fractional incidence chromatic number of any graph is at most Δ(''G'') + 20 log Δ(''G'') + 84. He has also proved the existence of graphs with fractional incidence chromatic number at least Δ(''G'') + Ω(log Δ(''G'')).

==Nordhaus–Gaddum inequality==
Let ''G'' be a graph with ''n'' vertices such that <math>G\neq K_n, \overline{K_n}</math> where <math>\overline{G}</math> denotes the complement of ''G''. Then <math>n + 2 \leq \chi_i(G) + \chi_{i}(\overline{G})\leq 2n-1.</math><ref name='sk' /> These bounds are sharp for all values of ''n''.

==Incidence coloring game==
[[Graph coloring game|Incidence coloring game]] was first introduced by S. D. Andres.<ref name='an'>Andres, S. D. (2009), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X07004866 The incidence game chromatic number]", Discrete Applied Mathematics 157, pp. 1980–1987</ref> It is the incidence version of the vertex coloring game, in which the incidences of a graph are colored instead of vertices. Incidence game chromatic number is the new parameter defined as a game-theoretic analogous of the incidence chromatic number.

The game is that two players, [[Alice and Bob]] construct a proper incidence coloring. The rules are stated below:
* Alice and Bob color the incidences of a graph ''G'' with a set ''k'' of colors.
* They are taking turns to provide a proper coloring to an uncolored incidence. Generally, Alice begins.
* In the case of an incidence that cannot be colored properly, then Bob wins.
* If every incidences of the graph is colored properly, Alice wins.

The incidence game chromatic number of a graph ''G'', denoted by <math>i_g(G)</math>, is the fewest colors required for Alice to win in an incidence coloring game. It unifies the ideas of incidence chromatic number of a graph and game chromatic number in case of an undirected graph. Andres found out that the upper bound for <math>i_g(G)</math> in case of ''k''-degenerate graphs is 2Δ + 4''k'' − 2. This bound was improved to 2Δ + 3''k'' − 1 in case of graphs in which Δ is at least 5''k''. The incidence game chromatic number of stars, cycles, and sufficiently large wheels are also determined.<ref name='an' /> John Y. Kim (2011) has found out the exact incidence game chromatic number of large paths and has given a correct proof of a result stated by Andres concerning the exact incidence game chromatic number of large wheels.<ref>Kim, J. Y. (2011), "[http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X10000028 The incidence game chromatic number of paths and subgraphs of wheels]", Discrete Applied Mathematics 159, pp. 683–694</ref>
